summary.text: A reflex is an involuntary, unplanned and nearly instantaneous response to a stimulus.
It travels along a neural pathway called a reflex arc: a stimulus starts a signal, which crosses a synapse to a motor neuron that produces the response.
The signals do not always travel to the brain, so many reflexes are automatic and need no conscious thought.

facts.label: Simplest type
facts.value: A short-latency reflex, with a single synapse

facts.label: Term introduced
facts.value: By physiologist Marshall Hall in the 19th century

facts.label: Concept first appears
facts.value: In the 17th century, with René Descartes

facts.label: Feline example
facts.value: The righting reflex reorients a falling cat

items.prompt: A doctor finds that a patient's tendon reflexes are all weaker than expected. Generally, where does that point?

options.label: A problem in the central nervous system
A problem in the peripheral nervous system
A problem in both equally
A problem in the stomach only

items.explain: Decreased reflexes generally indicate a peripheral problem, while lively or exaggerated reflexes point to a central one.

items.prompt: Your hand jerks off a hot pan before you even feel the heat. Why can that happen so fast?

options.label: The brain predicts the heat and acts early
Your muscles decide on their own to move
The signal does not always have to reach the brain
Pain nerves are faster than all other nerves

items.explain: Reflex signals do not always travel to the brain, so many reflexes are automatic responses that need no conscious thought.

items.prompt: In a reflex pathway, a stimulus sends a signal that crosses a synapse. Which cell does the signal reach to produce the response?

options.label: A motor neuron
The cerebral cortex
A sensory organ
A glial cell

items.explain: The signal is transferred across the synapse to a motor neuron, which evokes the target response.

items.prompt: A muscle stretched at rest contracts to resist the stretch. What happens to that resistance when you move voluntarily, such as reaching for a shelf?

options.label: It grows stronger to keep posture firm
It stays exactly the same
It locks the muscle until the movement ends
It is turned down or even reversed

items.explain: During voluntary movements the intensity of the reflex is reduced or its sign even reversed, which prevents the resistance from impeding the movement.

items.prompt: Descartes compared the body to a mechanical statue. What idea did the comparison illustrate?

options.label: Outside input can trigger responses automatically, without thought
The body can only move when a person decides to
Statues and bodies share one kind of nerve
Responses are random rather than predictable

items.explain: Descartes used the statue to explain how sensory input could trigger motor responses in a deterministic, automatic way without conscious thought.

items.prompt: Researchers want the simplest type of reflex, with only one junction in its pathway. Which type is it?

options.label: A long-latency reflex
An escape reflex
A short-latency reflex
A Golgi tendon reflex

items.explain: A short-latency reflex is the simplest type, with a single synapse; long-latency reflexes cross multiple synapses.

paragraphs.heading: An automatic response
paragraphs.text: A reflex is an involuntary, unplanned and almost instant response to a stimulus. Reflexes show up, simple or complex, in organisms that have a nervous system. Because the signals do not always go to the brain, many reflexes happen without any conscious thought.

paragraphs.heading: The reflex arc
paragraphs.text: A reflex runs along a nerve pathway called a reflex arc. A stimulus starts a nerve signal, which travels to a synapse, which is a junction on the pathway. There the signal passes to a motor neuron, which triggers the response. The simplest reflexes, called short-latency reflexes, have just one synapse on the path, while long-latency reflexes pass the signal across several synapses first.

paragraphs.heading: Built for survival
paragraphs.text: Many reflexes are tuned to help an organism survive and defend itself. The startle reflex gives an automatic reaction to something unexpected. The righting reflex of cats turns a falling cat's body so that it lands safely.

paragraphs.heading: Stretch and tendon reflexes
paragraphs.text: A stretch reflex is a muscle tightening in response to being stretched along its length. A tendon reflex is a muscle tightening when its tendon is struck. When a muscle at rest is stretched, the stretch reflex makes it contract and resist, which helps keep posture steady. During a deliberate movement, though, the reflex is turned down or even reversed, so that it does not get in the way.

paragraphs.heading: Reflexes in the clinic
paragraphs.text: Doctors often test reflexes to check the health of the nervous system. They typically grade each reflex from 0 to 4, where 2+ counts as normal. Some healthy people score 1+ on every reflex and others 3+. In general, weak reflexes point to a peripheral problem, while lively or exaggerated ones point to a central one.

paragraphs.heading: From Descartes to Hall
paragraphs.text: The idea of reflexes goes back to René Descartes in the 17th century. In his Treatise on Man, published after his death in 1664, he described how the body could act automatically in response to outside stimuli, comparing it to a mechanical statue. The word reflex itself came in the 19th century from the English physiologist Marshall Hall. In an 1833 paper he explained how the spinal cord carries out reflex actions apart from the brain's conscious control.
